title: Casino clay: white edge inserts, an inlay on the face
screen: Hands > Replayer, replay view (wagers, pot, flights)
observed: Today a wager's chip is 9.1 px across on a 402 x 874 phone (a board card is 34.8 px) and the pot's 11.4 px: a cylinder (face 0.724 of the width, edge 0.236) with twelve dark notches, a radial highlight and a white ring, in the app's own six colours. At most five chips in all; a wager is one column, the pot one column per colour.
change: The real tournament chip: each chip carries six white rectangular inserts round its edge, and they show on the stack as white blocks on the side and as a broken white ring on the top face, with a lighter inlay in the middle. The cylinder is lit from the left, so the side reads round instead of as a band.
why: Today's edge marks are dark notches on a dark chip, which disappear below 12 px; white inserts are the highest-contrast detail a chip can carry and read even at 9 px as "a casino chip".
risk: More gradient stops per disc (a pot of 25 discs is about 75 layers). Inserts on a white or yellow chip need a darker insert colour, a per-denomination exception.

title: Top view: the chip seen from above, stacks shingled

change: Drop the side view. Every chip is a full circle seen from straight above, six edge spots and a dashed inner ring, the way online rooms draw them; a stack is the same circle repeated a sixth of a chip lower each time, like chips pushed out in a short slide.
why: A circle is the largest a chip can be in its box: at the same width the face is 38% bigger than today's ellipse, so colour and spots carry twice the area.
risk: Loses the feeling of height: a stack of five looks like a smear rather than a column. Breaks the measured perspective the felt and cards were tuned to.

change: The colour system becomes materials: bronze 25, copper 100, silver 500, gold 1,000, rose gold 5,000, each a coin with a reeded edge, and the 25,000 is a rectangular platinum plaque, as high-roller rooms use. Value reads from the shape and the metal, not from a learned colour.

change: Today a wager is never more than five chips in all, so 12,000 and 30,000 can look alike. Draw the real breakdown, up to ten chips a stack, and when a stack would be taller the top chip carries a small "+".
why: A bigger bet looks bigger, which is the whole point of drawing chips. 38,000 shows its three 1,000s, which the five-chip cap drops today.

change: The chip's edge has four wide white quarters, not twelve fine notches, so when a chip turns in flight the rotation is visible; a stack is drawn as one element whose quarters shift by the amount.
why: Today's fine notches shimmer and alias when a chip moves, and a spinning chip with twelve marks looks still. Four marks give the eye something to follow.
risk: Bold quarters are louder at rest. The pattern repeats every 90 degrees, so a spin must be slower than a quarter-turn a frame or it strobes.

title: The pot as a pile, the wagers as stacks
screen: Hands > Replayer, replay view (wagers, pot, flights)
observed: Today a wager's chip is 9.1 px across on a 402 x 874 phone (a board card is 34.8 px) and the pot's 11.4 px: a cylinder (face 0.724 of the width, edge 0.236) with twelve dark notches, a radial highlight and a white ring, in the app's own six colours. At most five chips in all; a wager is one column, the pot one column per colour.
change: Wagers stay as neat stacks in front of the seats; once swept, the pot becomes a loose pile: short stacks of different heights leaning together, with a couple of chips lying flat in front, as chips land when a dealer pulls them in.
why: Separates the two kinds of money at a glance: what a player has put out (stacks) and what is in the middle (a pile). A growing pile is the best picture of a growing pot.
risk: Needs a new pot layout and new landing positions for the sweep and ship springs; harder to keep stable as the amount changes. Large effort.
